title: Artavon
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: In Jerusalem Talmud Peah, beginning of chapter 1, folio 3b, and Bereshit Rabbah, end of chapter 35: Artavlon sent our holy Rabbi one precious pearl, atimiton (great wealth), and Rabbi sent him one mezuzah. Rabbi wrote to him that the mezuzah is more valuable than the pearl, for the pearl he must guard, while the mezuzah guards its owner. Penei Moshe explains that he was an important Jew. Hyman judges that the Gaon designated שי״ד in Erekh Milin, entry Artavan, rightly identified him as a king of Persia in the time of Antoninus Commodus, the son of Antoninus, Rabbi’s friend.

Hyman reports that the Likkut on Zechariah 11 says that Rabbi, Antoninus and Charvan died in one month; Hyman identifies this Charvan as Artavan, who died in the year 504 of the Seleucid era (lishtarot). In Yoma 11a: “Rabbi Yehudah said: An incident with a certain Artavan” (Rashi explains: the man’s name) “who was checking mezuzot in the upper market of Tzippori; a quaestor found him and took a thousand zuz from him.” This Artavon is one particular man, and Hyman infers from the incident that he was an upright Jew.

The earlier notes record the limits of the evidence then available. Hyman’s print (vol. I, p. 243) reads שי״ר and names the pearl sender Artavon. The supplied text has שי״ד and Artavlon, both retained here. In the cited Erekh Milin (p. 196), Solomon Judah Löb Rapoport identifies Artaban as a Persian king called Wologeses III. Penei Moshe calls the figure in Peah an important Jew. Peah 1:1 describes the recipient as “our holy Rabbi,” while Bereshit Rabbah 35:3 calls him “our master.”

Yalkut Shimoni on Zechariah (§578) names Karbon, king of Persia, alongside Rabbi and Antoninus. Rapoport quotes the form Charvan, proposes Artaban or Ardaban, and argues for December 192 on his own reckoning. Hyman’s date of 504 in the documents era is retained as given. In Yoma 11a the consulted text reads Artavin. Rashi first explains it as the man’s name and also records the possibility that it refers to his occupation.
